summary:
AstroHealth Tracker is a browser-based decision-support dashboard that links space weather to the health of each crew member on the International Space Station. It combines the live ISS position, NASA DONKI solar events, NOAA SWPC data and each astronaut’s age and medical history into a personal 0–100 risk score with a 7-day forecast.

The challenge: radiation exposure changes by the minute with orbit position and solar activity, yet today radiation monitoring and vital-sign recording are separate tools, interpreted by experts on Earth. AstroHealth turns this data into action. It maps the radiation zones of the next three hours, finds safe spacewalk windows and simulates live vital signs with an ECG monitor. When a crew member’s risk reaches 70, an alarm opens automatically, naming who should help, what to do first, which medication the flight surgeon may approve and the earliest safe return date. Every alarm is logged, a one-page PDF report is one click away, and the app works offline in English and Turkish.

Why it matters: people with medical histories now fly to space, and on Moon and Mars missions crews must make health decisions on board when Earth is minutes away.
details:
AstroHealth Tracker is a decision-support dashboard that links space weather to the health of each individual crew member on the International Space Station.

What it does and how it works
A lightweight Python server collects live data every few minutes. It takes the ISS position from the Where the ISS at? API, and solar flares, coronal mass ejections, particle events and geomagnetic storms from NASA DONKI. It also takes Kp, GOES proton and X-ray data and forecasts from NOAA SWPC. For each of six fictional astronauts with different ages and medical histories, it combines three factors into a personal 0–100 risk score: where the ISS is (South Atlantic Anomaly, polar regions, equator), current space weather, and the person’s own condition. Each score comes with a 10-day history and a 7-day forecast. The web interface shows the radiation zones of the next three hours, a live map, safe spacewalk (EVA) windows, and simulated vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, SpO2, temperature) with a live ECG monitor.

Benefits
When a crew member’s risk reaches 70, an alarm opens automatically and closes again when the risk drops. The alarm names which crewmates should help, what to do first, which medication class the flight surgeon may approve, and the earliest safe date to return to Earth. Every alarm is written to a log file, and a one-page PDF report summarises the whole crew.

Intended impact
People with medical histories now fly to space. On Moon and Mars missions, crews will have to make health decisions on board, when Earth is minutes away. AstroHealth brings radiation data and personal health together in one place and turns them into a clear action.

Tools and technologies
Python 3 (standard library only, nothing to install), HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Chart.js, Leaflet and TopoJSON. It runs in a browser on any laptop. It also works offline from saved data backups, and it is available in English and Turkish.

Creativity
Existing tools keep radiation monitoring (NASA’s Space Radiation Analysis Group) and vital-sign recording (the Canadian Space Agency’s Bio-Monitor) separate, and experts on Earth interpret the data. We connect both to each person’s medical history and turn the result into a next step on board.

Factors our team considered

  • Safety and honesty: vital signs are simulated, astronauts are fictional, and medication is always the flight surgeon’s decision.
  • Reliability: the app opens instantly from cached data and keeps working without internet.
  • Transparency: a “Method and sources” page shows where every number comes from.
  • Explainability: risk and alarms follow clear rules, not a black-box model.

Use of AI
We used an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic) to help write the code, texts and presentation. The team designed, tested and reviewed the project.
